news.title: Prime minister did not attribute bad intentions to Alex Borg, deputy speaker rules
news.text:
Robert Abela did not attribute bad intentions to Alex Borg during a heated exchange in parliament on Monday, Deputy Speaker Bernard Grech has ruled.

The incident happened during a ministerial statement during parliament’s opening session in which the prime minister reported on his attendance at the UN General Assembly last month.

The words that Borg objected to came when Abela was reacting to the Opposition leader’s comment on government’s reluctance to implement the Daphne Caruana Galizia Public Inquiry recommendations. At one point, Abela noted that when government proposed changes to make tax evasion an administrative offence rather than strictly a criminal one, Borg had not been in parliament to vote.

“Why didn’t you come to vote? You know why you did not attend and for whom you did not show up. Don’t believe for one minute that if you point one finger at me, I will not point five fingers back at you… If you want, we can go outside and I will tell you for whom you did not want to come and vote…” Abela hit back.

Borg denied the accusation and challenged the prime minister to be transparent and mention the name.

Opposition Whip Ivan Castillo then objected to the prime minister’s words, insisting that he either substantiate the statement or withdraw it. This did not happen and Castillo asked the deputy speaker to rule on the issue in line with Standing Order 60.

Rule 60 states that no member of parliament should use offensive language when addressing other MPs. It also prohibits MPs from attributing bad intentions to each other.

The ruling was delivered today with Grech saying that Abela’s words did not fall foul of parliament’s rules.

“The Chair does not feel that the words over which the Opposition leader complained, fulfil the extremities required by Standing Order 60 to be construed as attributing bad intention to the Opposition leader’s behaviour by the prime minister,” Grech ruled.

Grech chaired parliament’s opening sessions this week since Speaker Carmelo Abela was away on official duties abroad.
news.summary: Deputy Speaker Bernard Grech rules against Opposition leader Alex Borg’s objection to words said by the prime minister during a heated parliamentary exchange
news.author: Kurt Sansone

news.title: ‘We cannot live in a society where officers going to help end up injured’:  Man charged over RIU altercation
news.text:
Joseph Scerri, 58, was arraigned in court on Wednesday over charges including insulting, threatening, or committing an offence against persons lawfully charged with a public service, as well as attacking or forcibly resisting the same officers.

He also faces charges of causing slight bodily harm.

On 4 October at 7:50pm, police were informed of a disturbance coming from a residence in Ħamrun. An RIU patrol was dispatched to the scene, where officers heard someone shouting for help from behind the front door.

As no one opened the door, officers forced their way inside, where they heard a man groaning in distress. The man was holding a pair of scissors and a piece of plastic and refused to cooperate with police until he was arrested on the spot.

The accused pleaded not guilty.

The defence requested bail, but the prosecution objected, citing the gravity of the charges and highlighting that RIU officers dispatched to assist ended up injured.

Pointing to the accused’s lengthy police conduct, the prosecution argued we cannot live in a society where an officer goes to help a citizen, only to end up getting injured.

Lawyer Martina Herrera remarked Scerri was never accused of violence in the past, and further argued that keeping him remanded in custody while court proceedings drag on will essentially serve no purpose.

The court rejected the request for bail, citing that the court has no peace of mind that the accused will adhere to conditions imposed on him.

Inspectors Miriam Lia and Sarah Kathleen Zerafa prosecuted, while lawyer Martina Herrera appeared for Scerri as legal aid.
news.summary: RIU officers forced entry after hearing cries for help, finding the man inside holding a pair of scissors
news.author: Kaylyn Linwood

news.title: Woman breaks down, begs magistrate not to send her to prison after Mater Dei fight with police officers
news.text:
A 24-year-old woman broke down in tears and begged a magistrate not to send her to prison on Wednesday, after being denied bail over an alleged fight with police and security officers at Mater Dei Hospital.

“Please magistrate, please don’t send me to prison,” the visibly distressed woman pleaded after Magistrate Ingrid Bianco ordered that she be remanded in custody.

“I’m going to take a turn for the worse in there, not receive help,” she told the court.

The magistrate sought to reassure the woman, telling her that her time in custody could serve as an opportunity for her to receive the assistance she needed.

Shanaia Taliana, an Qormi resident, who works as a salesperson, had earlier pleaded not guilty to a string of charges stemming from an incident at Mater Dei Hospital on Monday.

The court heard that the woman had gone to hospital after experiencing chest pain following cocaine consumption.

While receiving treatment, she allegedly wanted to leave the hospital to smoke a cigarette but was prevented from doing so by hospital staff.

An altercation subsequently broke out, prompting police officers to be called to the scene.

The prosecution said the woman became involved in a physical confrontation with two police officers and two security officers. All four allegedly suffered slight injuries during the incident.

She was subsequently arrested at around 9:50pm.

The woman was charged with disobeying and obstructing police officers in the exercise of their duties, insulting or threatening officers, disturbing the public peace by shouting and causing a disturbance, and uttering obscene language in public.

She was also charged with assaulting or violently resisting two police officers in the execution of their duties and slightly injuring two other people.

She pleaded not guilty to all charges.

Bail denied

The defence requested bail, but the prosecution objected.

Inspector Charlon Borg told the court while the prosecution sympathised with the accused, police officers were there for a reason and their authority had to be respected, particularly given that officers had allegedly been injured during the incident.

Legal aid lawyer Martina Herrera stressed the woman remained presumed innocent, telling the court that she had a stable job and fixed address and would abide by strict bail conditions.

The defence argued the court could also impose a protection order and treatment order if necessary.

Herrera further submitted the woman had apologised to the officers after realising what she had allegedly done, describing her as a young woman who supports herself.

The court, however, said it was not sufficiently reassured at this stage to release the woman on bail and ordered that she be remanded in custody.

It was upon hearing the decision that the woman became extremely emotional, crying loudly and repeatedly pleading with the magistrate not to send her to prison, “Please am I going to prison?... I didn't do it on purpose… please” she cried.

The court also issued a temporary supervision order.

The woman continued crying as she was escorted out of the courtroom.

Inspector Charlon Borg prosecuted.

Legal aid lawyer Martina Herrera represented the accused.

Magistrate Ingrid Bianco presided over the sitting.
news.summary: 24-year-old allegedly fought with two police officers and two security officers after being stopped from leaving the hospital to smoke a cigarette
news.author: Julia Dowling

news.title: Malta Chamber rejects Caruana claims that businesses favour cheap foreign labour over investment
news.text:
The Malta Chamber has rejected claims that businesses prefer low-cost third-country nationals (TCNs) over investment in capital, arguing Malta’s reliance on foreign labour is the result of a decade of state-backed economic policy rather than a reluctance by companies to modernise.

The Chamber was responding to concerns raised by Finance Minister Clyde Caruana over Malta’s rapid population growth and the pressure it is placing on the country’s infrastructure and quality of life.

While agreeing that population growth is creating “unnecessary and unsustainable pressure”, the Chamber said it disagreed with the minister’s characterisation of the private sector’s preference for foreign workers.

It argued that the claim misdiagnoses the root causes of Malta’s economic bottlenecks.

“The Finance Minister is well aware of how the current labour market framework was built,” the Chamber said, pointing to policies adopted under successive Labour administrations that promoted economic growth through an expansion of the foreign workforce.

Businesses are now operating within a regulatory and administrative framework designed for volume-driven growth, it said, despite repeated calls for Malta to shift from quantity towards quality and higher-value economic activity.

“It is neither fair nor accurate to place the full burden on employers now that physical and infrastructural limits are being reached,” the Chamber said.

The organisation also rejected the idea that employing TCNs is necessarily a cheap or straightforward option, pointing to the significant human resources administration and time involved in recruitment.

Growth driven primarily by more workers

The Chamber said Malta’s economic performance over the past decade highlights the extent to which growth has been driven by an expanding workforce rather than productivity.

Gross Value Added grew by 81.9%, it said, with 68.9% of that growth coming from an expansion of the labour force. Shifts towards higher-value-added sectors accounted for 9.9%, while actual productivity gains — measured as output per worker — contributed just 3.1%.

The Chamber said the model had been encouraged by state policy and that it was unrealistic to expect businesses to reverse a decade of workforce expansion on their own, particularly when government has repeatedly failed to implement proposals aimed at improving productivity.

The Malta Vision 2050 strategy itself recognises the need to move away from labour-driven growth towards an economy based on higher productivity, the Chamber noted.

It said the government should now ensure that the strategy’s key performance indicators are rigorously monitored and delivered rather than allowed to remain “aspirational talking points”.

Infrastructure and investment

The Chamber argued that a genuine shift towards a productivity-led economy would require significantly greater public investment.

Had government been pursuing a different economic direction, it said, there would have been decisive investment in measures to prevent recurring electricity disruptions, tackle traffic congestion, address disruption caused by abusive planning and construction, accelerate digitalisation across the public sector and private industry, and support reskilling and upskilling.

Instead, initiatives have repeatedly been delayed from one budget to another, undermining companies’ ability to plan their investments and budgets, it said.

The Chamber called for all fiscal incentives and grant support measures to be available from the beginning of each budget year, accompanied by clear and unambiguous timelines for disbursement.

It also argued that Malta’s existing fiscal and financial frameworks can discourage productive investment.

“Until state policy de-risks productive capital investment compared with flexible labour and speculative assets, businesses cannot realistically be expected to alter their behaviour in the quantum needed to bring real effective change,” it said.

A future budget should therefore realign government incentives, funding mechanisms and tax structures to reward automation, digitalisation and upskilling, with the aim of delivering sustained productivity gains.

Population growth outpacing productivity

The Chamber has repeatedly warned that an economic model based on continually increasing numbers of workers and visitors is unsustainable.

It said no level of infrastructure investment would be sufficient if demand continues to grow unchecked.

Malta’s population reached 588,254 at the end of 2025, with foreign residents accounting for about 31%, according to the figures cited by the Chamber. The population is projected to approach 636,000 by 2030, further intensifying pressure on a country that is already among the world’s most densely populated.

The Chamber also highlighted the contrast between Malta’s strong economic growth and weak productivity performance.

Real GDP increased by 22.9% between 2021 and 2025, making Malta the fastest-growing EU economy over the period, it said. However, real GDP per hour worked fell by 0.2%, placing Malta 21st among the 27 EU member states for productivity growth.

The figures, the Chamber said, point to the need for a decisive response from the state on both infrastructure and productivity rather than a shift of responsibility onto employers.

Public sector bottlenecks

The Chamber also rejected the suggestion that businesses continue to seek foreign workers simply because they are unwilling to modernise.

Companies that have invested in automation, lean processes and digital tools are achieving efficiency gains, it said, but these gains are frequently being eroded by bottlenecks elsewhere in the economy.

These include delays in public administration when processing applications, queries and paperwork, inconsistencies between government departments and the absence of “once-only” systems that prevent businesses and citizens from repeatedly providing the same information.

The Chamber also argued that continued public-sector recruitment is contributing to the demand for workers, particularly during periods of increased hiring ahead of elections.

It called for an independent audit of all government departments and entities to identify structural redundancies, streamline bureaucratic layers and determine whether surplus capacity exists.

The objective, it said, should be to improve efficiency rather than expand headcount.

The review should include a comprehensive assessment of human resource requirements across the public sector, alongside a transition programme to facilitate the secondment or redeployment of surplus public-sector personnel into private-sector roles.

A productivity-led economy

The Malta Chamber said it remains ready to work with both the government and the Opposition on an evidence-based plan for Malta’s economic future.

Such a plan should combine infrastructure investment, simpler administration and well-designed incentives to ensure that economic growth is increasingly driven by productivity rather than population and workforce growth.

The Chamber’s position is that businesses cannot be expected to deliver that transition alone.

Instead, it argues, government policy must make productive investment in automation, digitalisation, skills and capital more attractive than continued reliance on additional labour.

Only then, it said, can Malta move from an economic model based on increasing headcount towards one built on higher productivity and greater value-added growth.
news.summary: Malta Chamber says businesses operating within a regulatory and administrative framework designed for volume-driven growth, despite repeated calls for Malta to shift from quantity towards quality and higher-value economic activity
news.author: Karl Azzopardi

news.title: ORNIS approves government proposal to cut penalties for hunting illegalities
news.text:
The ORNIS Committee has voted in favour of proposed changes to fines and penalties under Malta’s bird protection legislation, despite objections from BirdLife Malta, which has warned the amendments could weaken the consequences faced by those who illegally target protected birds.

The vote saw BirdLife Malta vote against the proposals, while the Environment and Resources Authority (ERA) abstained and called for further discussion. The Federation for Hunting and Conservation – Malta (FKNK) voted in favour, while attaching a proviso concerning offences involving protected birds listed under Schedules 1 and 9.

The outcome now leaves the government to decide on its next steps.

The vote followed a lengthy discussion during which BirdLife Malta raised concerns about how the proposed legislative changes were being presented to the committee.

At its previous meeting, a lawyer representing the government had presented the proposed amendments to ORNIS members. At Tuesday’s meeting, members were asked to vote on those proposals, which had been presented across five slides.

BirdLife Malta argued committee members should instead have been provided with the actual proposed wording of the amended legislation before being asked to vote. The organisation said this would be the normal approach when considering changes to legislation.

BirdLife Malta also sought clarification on the position of the Wild Birds Regulation Unit (WBRU), particularly because the unit had not been present during the previous discussion on the proposals.

Following the discussion, the chairperson proceeded with the vote and allowed committee members to attach provisos to their positions.

BirdLife Malta voted against the proposed changes, while ERA abstained and requested further discussion. FKNK supported the proposals but said that, in cases involving offences against protected birds listed under Schedules 1 and 9, a magistrate should not be obliged to revoke the offender’s licence.

Instead, FKNK argued that licence revocation should remain at the discretion of the magistrate, depending on the circumstances of each case.

BirdLife Malta said it was “highly disappointed” that FKNK had not sought to keep the existing fines and penalties for offences involving protected birds under Schedules 1 and 9 unchanged.

The conservation organisation argued that by backing the proposed changes, FKNK had indicated its support for reducing the fines and penalties for such offences.

“By supporting the proposals, FKNK has clearly indicated that it is in favour of reducing these fines and penalties, thereby representing the interests of those who break the law and hunt protected species,” BirdLife Malta said, adding that this was “far from a zero-tolerance stance”.

At the same time, BirdLife Malta noted that FKNK appeared to accept the principle that licence revocation should remain among the sanctions available for such offences, even if it wants magistrates to retain discretion over whether the sanction is imposed.

BirdLife Malta reiterated its position that offences involving the illegal killing of protected birds constitute serious environmental crimes and that existing fines and penalties should not be weakened.

The organisation also called on the government to ensure that any changes to environmental legislation are subject to proper public participation and consultation, in line with Malta’s obligations under the Aarhus Convention.

It further said that any amendments to the Conservation of Wild Birds Regulations should take into account Malta’s international obligations to combat illegal hunting and trapping, including commitments arising from the Bern Convention’s Rome Strategy Plan and the transposition of the EU’s Environmental Crime Directive.

BirdLife Malta said neither of these considerations had been addressed during the ORNIS Committee’s discussions.

The organisation is now calling on the government not to bow to pressure to weaken the penalties faced by people who illegally target protected birds.
news.summary: BirdLife Malta votes against, FKNK approves and Environment and Resources Authority (ERA) abstains on government proposals slashing fines and penalties for hunting illegalities
news.author: Karl Azzopardi

news.title: PN backs call for free chemotherapy for cancer patients under government’s medicines formulary
news.text:
Cancer patients should have access to chemotherapy free of charge under the government’s medicines formulary, the Malta Union of Midwives and Nurses (MUMN) has said, as the Partit Nazzjonalista pledged to keep the issue a priority.

During a pre-budget meeting with MUMN, Opposition Leader and PN leader Alex Borg said the union’s proposals closely aligned with those of the Nationalist Party and stressed the importance of ensuring patients receive a more efficient healthcare service.

MUMN has put forward three proposals for the forthcoming Budget, with the first calling for chemotherapy to be included on the government formulary. This would ensure cancer patients do not have to plead for treatment or pay tens of thousands of euros from their own pockets.

The union is also calling for designated cubicles in the Emergency Department to be allocated to cancer patients, alongside a fast-track system to reduce the risk of further health complications caused by infections they could contract while spending long periods in waiting areas.

Its third proposal is to overhaul the waiting-list system so patients are informed when they are placed on a waiting list and are immediately given a provisional date for their appointment or operation.

Speaking during the meeting, held at the PN leader’s new office at the AŻAD building in Valletta, Borg said all three proposals were important to providing patients with a more efficient service.

He also addressed the working conditions of nurses and midwives, saying the healthcare sector depended on them and that they should have not only adequate salaries but also working conditions that allow them to maintain a good quality of life.

Borg said the PN would continue to push for improvements to healthcare infrastructure, including strengthening the Emergency Department, as well as greater transparency over waiting lists.

He said many of the issues discussed during the meeting had already featured in the PN’s electoral manifesto for the last election.

Shadow Finance Minister Adrian Delia, Shadow Minister for the Economy, Technology and Strategic Projects Darren Carabott, and Shadow Health Minister Stephen Spiteri also attended the meeting.
news.summary: Opposition leader Alex Borg and MPs meet with Malta Union of Midwives and Nurses in pre-Budget meeting
news.author: Karl Azzopardi

news.title: Chef handed suspended sentence after using forged stamps to stay in Malta with son
news.text:
A 53-year-old chef has admitted in court to using fake passport stamps to extend his stay in Malta so he could remain with his son.

The court granted a request for a ban on the publication of the accused's name to safeguard the man and his family in Malta.

The incident unfolded on 6 October, when officers at Malta International Airport inspected the man’s passport as he was preparing to board a flight bound for Belgrade. During the routine check, officers noticed suspicious markings and identified two forged stamps.

He was immediately placed under arrest at the airport.

During police questioning, the man cooperated fully with investigators. He explained that he had obtained the forged stamps in order to overstay his visa and remain in Malta to be with his son, adding that he was finally returning to his home country now that his son had reached 18 years of age. Police confirmed that although the accused was using the falsified stamps, he had not produced them himself.

Appearing in court following his arrest, the accused registered an early guilty plea, telling the court: "I made a terrible mistake, I am guilty."

In defence submissions, his legal counsel emphasised that the 53-year-old has an otherwise clean police record and had never had any previous run-ins with the law. Citing his full cooperation with police from the outset, his genuine remorse, and his immediate admission of guilt, the defence recommended that the court hand down a suspended sentence.

The court sentenced the man to two years imprisonment, suspended for four years.

Magistrate Ingrid Bianco presided.

Inspector Ylenia Xerri prosecuted, while lawyer Gianluca Cappitta represented the accused.
news.summary: 53-year-old chef has admits to using fake passport stamps to extend his stay in Malta so he could remain with his son
news.author: Kaylyn Linwood

news.title: Free animal first aid courses announced between October and November
news.text:
The government has announced the dates and locations of free Animal First Aid courses, which will run in different localities from 16 October to 28 November.

The courses will teach residents how to respond when an animal is in an emergency, with participants receiving basic, practical training in choking, animal CPR, wound care, and poisoning. 

“When an animal is in an emergency situation, the first few minutes can be crucial. Through these courses, we aim to equip people with practical knowledge that can help them act safely and responsibly until the necessary veterinary assistance is provided,” said Parliamentary Secretary Alicia Bugeja Said.

She said that through this education, people will be provided with the necessary tools, to strengthen a culture of responsibility, care, and respect towards animals.

The initiative is a collaboration between the Parliamentary Secretariat for Animal Protection and the Ministry for Local Government and Public Works. 

Local Government Minister Alison Zerafa Civelli said 26 Local Councils have expressed interest in participating in this initiative, demonstrating the importance of continuing to create learning opportunities that are accessible and close to residents.

"Animal welfare begins with awareness, responsibility, and preparation; through this collaboration between the Government, Local Councils, and the Animal Welfare Directorate, we are bringing this knowledge closer to our communities.” 

The schedule covers eight sessions, each hosted by one council and open to residents of nearby localities. Bugeja Said said the courses show the government is investing in education and awareness in communities as well as in animal protection.

Qualified educators selected by the Animal Welfare Directorate will deliver the training and the courses will run as follows:

 Qala (Qala, Xagħra, Għarb): 16 October 2026, 3pm to 7pm
 Bormla (Ħal Tarxien, Bormla, Birgu): 17 October 2026, 8am to 12pm
 Floriana (Msida, Santa Venera, Tal-Pietà, Ħamrun, Floriana): 24 October 2026, 8am to 12pm
 Fgura (Fgura, Paola, Santa Luċija): 31 October 2026, 8am to 12pm
 Rabat (Rabat, Ħ'Attard, Ħal Balzan, Ħal Lija, Ħad-Dingli): 7 November 2026, 8am to 12pm
 Pembroke (Swieqi, San Ġiljan, Pembroke): 12 November 2026, 1pm to 5pm
 Marsaskala (Qrendi, Marsaskala, Marsaxlokk): 21 November 2026, 8am to 12pm
 Mellieħa (Mellieħa): 28 November 2026, 10:30am to 2:30pm
news.summary: Courses will teach residents how to respond when an animal is in an emergency, with participants receiving basic, practical training in choking, animal CPR, wound care, and poisoning between 16 October and 28 November

news.title: European Parliament Urges Tougher but Open EU Approach to China
news.text:
The European Parliament on Wednesday called for the European Union to keep up dialogue with China while taking a firmer line on trade, security and human rights, saying relations have reached a critical point.

Lawmakers adopted the recommendation, addressed to the other EU institutions, by a vote of 454-86, with 110 abstentions. It says the EU’s interest lies in reinforcing a multilateral world and stresses the importance of talks with China on global challenges, peace and security, climate and human rights.

The lawmakers blamed the strain in relations on China’s unfair economic practices and its position on Russia’s war against Ukraine. They said they were deeply concerned by verified reports that the Chinese military has trained Russian military personnel to fight in Ukraine. The EU should coordinate with the United States, G7 members and other like-minded partners, they said, and encourage China to use its influence on Russia to help end the war.

Trade and dependencies

Lawmakers said urgent action is needed against the weaponization of the EU’s overreliance on China. They called for a rigorous de-risking strategy focused on critical raw materials, medicines, batteries, electric vehicles, information and communication technology, semiconductors and other strategic sectors. They also urged stronger investment screening and better protection of critical technologies, infrastructure and supply chains.

Parliament identified China’s industrial overcapacity, state subsidies and restrictions on European firms’ access to the Chinese market as growing challenges to the EU economy. Lawmakers demanded reciprocity and a level playing field in trade and investment, and they backed proportionate EU action if China fails to open its internal markets.

The recommendation also calls for stronger Global Gateway partnerships to offer a credible alternative to China’s Belt and Road Initiative, particularly in Africa and Latin America.

Taiwan, security and human rights

The recommendation reaffirms the EU’s One China policy while opposing any unilateral change to the status quo in Taiwan by force or coercion.

Lawmakers called for stronger resilience against cyberattacks, foreign interference, espionage and hybrid threats. They also demanded a reinforced human rights dialogue and more pressure on China over repression, forced labor and policies in Tibet and Xinjiang.

Parliament expressed deep concern over China’s adoption of the Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress, saying it could further institutionalize assimilationist policies. Lawmakers also called for the unconditional release of political prisoners.

“Today’s majority marks a turning point in Europe’s China policy,” said Hilde Vautmans, a Belgian lawmaker with the Renew group who wrote the report. She cited a Franco-German initiative this week as a sign that “a broad EU consensus is emerging on the need for a more balanced economic relationship with China.”

Vautmans said she hopes Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič will take that message to Beijing on Thursday. “We want cooperation with China where possible, while standing firm on our security and values,” she said. “As long as fundamental differences persist, systemic rivalry will also be part of our relationship.”

Three parliamentary delegations visited China between March and June 2026, and a fourth is expected later in October. Direct contacts between the European Parliament and Chinese authorities resumed last year after being effectively frozen since 2021. That year, the Chinese government imposed sanctions on several lawmakers in response to EU human rights sanctions against Chinese officials and organizations.

news.title: Turkey sending technical, defensive support to Saudi Arabia to help fight Houthis
news.text:
Turkey is sending mainly defensive and ​technical support to Saudi Arabia to help it fight Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis, two officials said on Wednesday, ‌after the NATO member and Pakistan pledged to act on the collective defence commitment of their newly formed alliance.

Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member constituted an attack on all. They have been working ​to set the parameters of the new alliance and have held political and military meetings in response to the Houthi attacks.

On ​Monday, the countries said they had agreed to move immediately to implement their collective defence ⁠commitments and ensure the “rapid deployment” of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.

Turkey, which has NATO’s second-largest army and a ​robust defence industry, has condemned the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, voiced willingness to help meet Riyadh’s technical military needs, and agreed ​to join a Saudi-led coalition to ensure navigational safety in the Red Sea.

A Turkish official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the support expected from Turkey was only in the form of military equipment, intelligence sharing, and weapons systems, adding that no other form of deployment had ​taken place as part of the alliance so far.

DRONE OPERATORS, FINE-TUNING DEFENSIVE MEASURES

Turkey’s Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan attends the Mecca defense pact meeting between Turkey, Saudi Arabia ​and Pakistan in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, October 5, 2026. Saudi Press Agency/Handout via REUTERS Purchase Licensing Rights, opens new tab

Officials have said that Turkish support for Saudi ​Arabia — including air defence systems — would largely be in a bilateral capacity for now, as Turkey’s parliament has not officially ratified the joint pact. ‌The amount ⁠and nature of the support would increase after ratification, they have said.

A US official briefed on the matter said that Turkey had so far decided to send capabilities that were broadly defensive, including strategic planning support and help with logistics. The official said the assistance included drone operators and help with fine-tuning defensive measures, as well as intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance.

Turkish Foreign ​Minister Hakan Fidan, speaking to ​state media after an extraordinary ⁠meeting of the Mecca alliance in Riyadh, said the sides had discussed what support to provide Saudi Arabia to help its defensive capabilities.

“We had our Defence Minister and Chief of ​General Staff with us, and they especially provided very fruitful views on military issues, operational ​issues, and technical ⁠matters,” he said on Monday.

Pakistani and regional officials have said Ankara and Islamabad have provided Saudi Arabia with military equipment that the kingdom is using in Yemen.

This week, Yemeni government forces with Saudi-led coalition air support launched a counter-offensive to recapture strategic territory near ⁠the Bab ​el-Mandeb Strait, an international shipping route for energy exports and other trade.

Officials ​had told Reuters last week that Saudi Arabia was planning an offensive against the Houthis, with options being considered including a coastal push to secure the Red ​Sea shipping route or an assault on multiple fronts.

Source: Reuters

news.title: New Maltese historical novel brings sixteenth-century Birgu to life before the Great Siege
news.text:
Maltese author Stephen Magri will publish his debut historical novel, Thumasi Zahra - A Soul Taught Mercy Before the Great Siege, as an eBook on 9 October 2026.

Set principally in sixteenth-century Birgu in the years before the Great Siege of 1565, the novel approaches one of Malta’s most familiar historical periods from an unusual direction: through the lives of ordinary people before the siege itself begins.

At the centre of the story is Thumasi Zahra, the son of a harbour labourer. Growing up among dockworkers, galleys, captives, noble households and the Knights of St John, Thumasi discovers an unusual gift for languages. That ability gradually draws him beyond the world into which he was born and brings him into contact with people of very different rank and experience.

Yet the novel is concerned as much with conscience as with history. Thumasi is raised in a deeply Catholic household and learns early that mercy is easier to praise than to practise. As a child, troubled by the sight of chained captives in the harbour, he begins asking questions for which the adults around him do not always have comfortable answers.

His parish priest later teaches him the words Manus Christi — “the hands of Christ” — an idea that remains with him: faith does not remove the obligation to act, and mercy may have to work through ordinary human hands.

As Thumasi grows older, his life becomes increasingly entangled with a noble household and with Lucia di Santocanale, a young woman whose social world is closed to him by class and family expectation. Their growing attachment develops quietly against the rigid distinctions of sixteenth-century society and the hostility of Lucia’s brother.

The story also brings Thumasi into the orbit of the Knights of St John. Training, harbour work and an episode at sea force him to confront the difference between courage and violence, while the political and military pressures surrounding Malta begin to gather in the background.

Rather than treating the years before the Great Siege merely as a prelude to battle, Thumasi Zahra seeks to recreate Birgu as a lived place: its streets, harbour, churches, households, work, social divisions and moral tensions.

“Malta’s history is often told through commanders, battles and fortifications,” Magri said. “I wanted to look at the same world from below — through a family that works, worries, prays and tries to live decently while larger historical forces are beginning to move around them.”

The novel is the first volume of the planned Thumasi Zahra trilogy.
news.summary: Maltese author Stephen Magri will publish his debut historical novel, Thumasi Zahra - A Soul Taught Mercy Before the Great Siege, as an eBook on 9 October 2026

news.title: WATCH | Moroccan community, friends bid emotional farewell to murder victim Abdellatif Oumakhlouf
news.text:
There was little that needed to be said when the coffin holding Abdellatif Oumakhlouf's body was brought outside. Placed beside the wall outside the mortuary, it was surrounded by the people who had come to say goodbye to the young man who was murdered in Paceville.

Members of Malta’s Moroccan community, friends, his uncle, and colleagues from Attard Brothers, where he worked, gathered in prayer, standing around the coffin before it began its final journey home. Oumakhlouf's body will be taken back to his family in Morocco.

The gathering on Wednesday was marked by grief, but also by solidarity. Among those present was Dounia Borg, the president of the Morroccan community in Malta, who has been closely involved in the efforts surrounding the body's repatriation. She thanked members of the Moroccan community and the victim’s friends for coming together, as well as everyone who helped make it possible for his body to be returned to his family.

She expressed particular gratitude towards the Moroccan representative in Rome for the assistance provided throughout the process. In a moment shaped both by faith and tradition, Borg explained that the prayers around the coffin were attended by the men of the community.

But beyond the formalities of repatriation, Wednesday’s farewell became something more personal; an opportunity for those who knew him to speak about the man behind the tragedy.

Oumakhlouf's uncle struggled with emotion as he described his nephew simply as a good young man—someone who did not go looking for trouble. He also thanked Malta’s Moroccan community for the support it had offered the family throughout the ordeal, saying that what had been achieved would not have been possible without the people who came together to help.

For a family grieving from another country, that community became the hands on the ground in Malta—helping to ensure that their loved one could finally be brought home.

A close friend of the victim was equally emotional. He described Oumakhlouf as a person without malice, someone he remembered simply as a very good human being.

And behind the life he had built in Malta, his friend said, was a personal ambition; he wanted to help his family. That was what he had been working towards, the friend said.

Oumakhlouf's employer spoke with the same sense of loss. “We lost one of our family,” the Attard Brothers representative said. “We are a family here and we will miss him.”

The words captured what was visible outside the mortuary—people who crossed Oumakhlouf's path converging in one place to bid him farewell him. And as Malta prepares to return him to the home he had hoped to support, those who had become his community here came together for one final act of friendship.

On Friday, Oumakhlouf's body is expected to be back in Morocco, where his family will finally be able to receive him and lay him to rest.

The farewell ceremony comes little more than a week after Oumakhlouf, 31, was found dead at Spinola Gardens in St Julian’s following an early-morning altercation.

Police investigations, aided by CCTV footage from the surrounding area, led to the arrest of 27-year-old Polish tourist Sebastian Malinowski. He has since been charged with Oumakhlouf’s wilful homicide and grievous bodily harm resulting in death, charges to which he has pleaded not guilty. He remains in custody while the case continues before the courts.
news.summary: Friends, relatives, colleagues and members of Malta’s Moroccan community gathered in prayer at the hospital mortuary on Wednesday to give murder victim Abdellatif Oumakhlouf a dignified send-off • 'We lost one of our family'
news.author: Jaelle Borg

news.title: Paramount-Warner Bros merger – How the deal could affect you
news.text:
It has been months in the making but Paramount Skydance has finally completed its $110bn (£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery.

The deal welds two legacy Hollywood powerhouses, uniting franchises like Harry Potter and Game of Thrones, into an entertainment behemoth named Skydance.

Yet behind this milestone lies strict rules about what the combined business can and cannot do – from how many films it must produce a year to the editorial independence of its newsroom.

Here are four ways this could affect you and the movies, TV and news you watch.

1. Streaming prices may rise

Warner Bros owns HBO Max, home to The Sopranos, House of the Dragon and Euphoria among others. Meanwhile, Paramount Skydance has Paramount+, which streams the likes of Yellowstone, Parks and Recreation and NCIS.

Combining HBO Max and Paramount+ into a single platform or bundle will likely squeeze subscribers’ wallets over time.

While existing subscribers to both might enjoy short-term savings, analysts expect overall prices to rise as the combined giant seeks profitability.

The merged company, Skydance, carries a massive $80bn in debt from the deal, even as executives target $6bn in annual cost savings.

Analysts warn that consumers will ultimately bear the financial burden of the $110bn deal.

Mike Proulx, research director at Forrester, noted that with streaming services constantly raising fees to increase profitability and Skydance saddled with massive debt, price increases are likely to come.

While viewers will gain access to a broader catalog, as Skydance shifts toward a Paramount+ and HBO Max bundle rather than a single app, Proulx warns that “it’s far-fetched to think it’ll prevent downstream price hikes”.

2. More film releases

As part of a settlement deal with US states who had objected to the merger, Paramount Skydance has agreed to release a set number of films every year for the next five years.

For the first two years, that’s 30 movies annually, and for the remaining period it has to release 32 films each year.

That’s 156 movies in total – and the majority have to be “wide releases,” meaning they must be shown in cinemas.

The merged studio must also release at least four independent films each year.

If Skydance misses its movie quota, it could be forced to sell its 49% stake in Miramax – the studio co-founded by disgraced Hollywood mogul Harvey Weinstein.

Breanne Gilliam, a corporate lawyer at Maddin Hauser, said the film commitment is meaningful, even if it comes with an expiration date.

“Once those obligations expire, the company will have far more flexibility,” she said.

“Temporary rules cannot permanently fix a structural market shift”.

Once the five-year deal ends, Skydance could follow rivals like Disney and Netflix by prioritizing streaming over cinema.

As Disney’s $71bn buyout of 21st Century Fox in 2019 proved, mega-deals can lead to fewer films in cinemas.

Before the acquisition, 20th Century Fox routinely released 12 to 17 movies annually in theatres, but under Disney that slate scaled down to just three to six a year.

3. Hollywood jobs could be hit

For those working behind the scenes, the merger of two historic studios has been described as a “disaster” by those on the ground.

Actors and writers recently gathered at Paramount Studios in Los Angeles to oppose the deal, accusing regulators of failing to protect industry livelihoods.

Criminal Minds star Kirsten Vangsness told the BBC she was “heartbroken”.

“It’s people that make this city,” she said. “It’s people that make entertainment, it’s the everyday creatives that this industry is built on – this is who it hurts.”

A report by consultancy CVL Economics for LA County estimated the merger could eliminate roughly 4,500 direct film and TV jobs, while causing $1.26bn in lost wages over three years.

The blow could hit a region that has already lost roughly a third of its film and TV workforce, about 50,000 jobs, since 2022.

Syleecia Thompson, a business professor at National University, said that “it hits small businesses, vendors, caterers and local communities”.

She warned that Hollywood may become less of a “single location” and more of a “dispersed network.”

Although the settlement establishes a workforce fund to retrain displaced workers, lawyers note it does not block job cuts.

“Nothing in the settlement limits layoffs,” attorney Gilliam added.

4. CNN and CBS could change

To address concerns over journalistic independence at CNN and CBS, the settlement creates a news editorial independence board that will be appointed directly by Paramount.

The $110bn deal brings two major US television news operations under a single corporate roof. Before the deal, Paramount owned CBS News, and Warner Bros. owned CNN.

Both networks have faced intense political pressure – CNN was one of a handful of news organisations banned from the White House by President Donald Trump – as well as leadership shifts amid broader industry consolidation.

Paramount chief executive David Ellison has asked CNN boss Mark Thompson – the former director general of the BBC – to remain at the helm after the takeover closes. CBS News’s editor-in-chief Bari Weiss will remain in her role.

Yet as Paramount targets billions in cost cuts across the merged company, staff fear the consolidation will trigger significant job losses at CNN and CBS.

Beyond potential workforce reductions, media advocates and legal experts remain deeply skeptical about whether it can ensure newsroom freedom.

Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at Freedom of the Press Foundation, described the Paramount-appointed board as “worthless”.

“The board creates the same First Amendment problems it claims to solve, the government meddling in news,” Stern said.

Gilliam agrees paper promises mean little without real authority. “An oversight board only has as much power as the agreement gives it. Oversight without authority is just observation,” she said.

The deal welds two legacy Hollywood powerhouses, uniting franchises like Harry Potter and Game of Thrones, into an entertainment behemoth named Skydance. Yet behind this milestone lies strict rules about what the combined business […]

news.title: Centric and Talexio partner to connect Odoo ERP with Maltese payroll platform
news.text:
Malta-based technology company Centric has partnered with HR and payroll platform Talexio to integrate Odoo ERP with Talexio’s payroll software, giving businesses a new way to connect their enterprise resource planning and payroll systems.

Odoo is an all-in-one business management platform that brings functions including accounting, sales, purchasing, inventory and other business operations together in a single system. The new integration allows Odoo users to connect their existing setup with Talexio payroll, creating a smoother flow of payroll-related data between the two platforms.

For businesses seeking a payroll solution built around Maltese requirements, Talexio combines local payroll expertise with its HR and payroll platform. The integration allows companies to add Talexio payroll to an existing Odoo environment without having to create a separate manual process for transferring information.

Instead of exporting data, re-entering it and checking it before each payroll run, organisations can transfer information between the two systems with minimal intervention. This removes the need for double data entry, reduces the risk of errors during data transfer and means businesses do not have to migrate existing payroll records from Talexio to Odoo.

"At Centric, we believe technology should work around the business, not the other way around," said Kieran Sant, CEO of Centric. "By connecting Odoo with Talexio, businesses can keep the payroll system they already know and trust while removing the manual work between the two platforms. It’s a simple integration, but one that can make a real difference to day-to-day operations."

Businesses can configure the integration according to their own processes. Data can be transferred automatically through an application programming interface, or API, or exported as a structured Excel file for teams that prefer to review information before it reaches payroll.

Transfers can also be scheduled around regular payroll cycles or triggered manually when required. This gives businesses the flexibility to support highly automated payroll processes while also allowing organisations to retain a review step where needed.

Mark Camilleri Gambin, CEO and co-founder of Talexio, said the integration gives clients greater flexibility in how they manage their systems.

"This integration brings a great level of flexibility for our clients," he said. "Odoo provides a robust ERP foundation, while Talexio ensures payroll can be processed accurately, on time and in line with the relevant legislation. By connecting the two systems, businesses can avoid manual processes and create a smoother flow of information between their ERP and payroll. This supports our mission to improve employee and organisational wellbeing by removing unnecessary friction from everyday operations."

The partnership brings together Centric’s expertise in Odoo implementation and integrations with Talexio’s experience in HR and payroll technology. Centric supports businesses across Malta with Odoo implementation, system customisation, data migration, training and ongoing local support.

Talexio supports more than 2,000 organisations and has more than 27,000 active users on its HR platform. Its modular system covers core HR, time and attendance, performance management and payroll, allowing organisations to use the modules they need and integrate them with other business systems.

The company’s payroll software processes more than 34,500 payslips each month and is designed around Maltese tax, social security and statutory requirements. The platform combines local payroll expertise with a flexible HR system that can be integrated into a company’s wider technology environment.

The new Odoo-Talexio integration gives businesses a practical way to connect two systems they already rely on, reducing manual processes while keeping payroll within a platform tailored to the Maltese market.
news.summary: Malta-based technology company Centric partners with HR and payroll platform Talexio to integrate Odoo ERP with Talexio’s payroll software, giving businesses a new way to connect their enterprise resource planning and payroll systems

news.title: Malta registers Europe’s largest annual increase in tourism GDP contribution in 2025
news.text:
Malta recorded the highest annual increase in the Travel and Tourism sector’s contribution to GDP among European economies in 2025, according to the latest research by the World Travel and Tourism Council (WTTC).

The contribution grew by 16.8% compared to the European average of 2.6%, with data also showing that the European tourism industry is projected to grow 2.5% in 2026. 

Despite geopolitical and economic uncertainty, WTTC forecasts global Travel & Tourism growth of 2.5% in 2026, ahead of the broader economy. Europe is expected to grow faster: international visitor spending by 5.8%, leisure travel spending by 3.1%, and business travel spending by 4.2%.

The sector is expected to contribute $4.9 billion to Malta’s economy, accounting for 16.9% of GDP and supporting more than one in five jobs.

At the Summit, more than 100 speakers will discuss topics such as investment, connectivity, innovation, artificial intelligence, skills and the workforce, destination competitiveness, and sustainability.

Speaking at the opening of the summit on Wednesday, Minister for Tourism Jo Etienne Abela said the Summit offers Malta, alongside international leaders, an opportunity to discuss concrete solutions to the sector's realities, including the need for increased investment, improved connectivity, technological innovation, skills development, and sustainable growth.

He reiterated that for Malta, hosting the WTTC Global Summit is more than just an international conference. “It is an opportunity for the country to showcase its progress, share its vision for the future, and further strengthen ties with leaders and organisations shaping the future of the global tourism industry.”

He highlighted that hosting the WTTC Global Summit recognises Malta’s standing as a world-class tourist destination.

“Today, Malta is not simply welcoming the tourism world; it is serving as a platform where the sector’s future direction is being discussed,” he concluded.

WTTC Chairman Manfredi Lefebvre said Malta is an ideal host for the Summit because of its commitment to the sector, while emphasising the importance of international leaders strengthening collaboration and creating new initiatives that continue to drive growth, investment, and opportunities.

news.title: Man granted bail over Marsa hit-and-run which left pedestrian grievously injured
news.text:
A 41-year-old man has been granted bail after being charged over a hit-and-run in Marsa which left a pedestrian grievously injured.

Justin Vella pleaded not guilty to 12 charges, including grievously injuring the pedestrian, speeding, driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs, refusing a breathalyser test, committing a number of traffic violations and leaving the scene without assisting the victim.

The court heard that Vella allegedly ran a red light before hitting the 41-year-old Bangladeshi pedestrian on Triq Diċembru 13.

Prosecutors said eyewitnesses reported that the driver did not simply flee after the collision, but later returned to the scene.

He allegedly got out of the vehicle before getting back in and speeding away once again while police officers were already at the scene.

A medical team treated the pedestrian at the scene before he was taken by ambulance to Mater Dei Hospital, where his injuries were certified as grievous.

The incident occurred at around 10pm on 20 September. Police investigations, aided by recorded footage and eyewitness accounts, eventually led officers to a BMW parked in Marsaskala, where Vella was arrested. Police said the vehicle had lost a side mirror in the collision, which was recovered from the scene.

Vella was initially denied bail when he was arraigned before Magistrate Donatella Frendo Dimech, after the prosecution raised concerns over the nature of the alleged incident and the risk of evidence being tampered with while key witnesses had yet to testify.

However, on Wednesday morning, the case was heard before Judge Neville Camilleri in the Criminal Court, who granted Vella bail against a €5,000 deposit and a €10,000 personal guarantee.

He was also placed under a daily curfew and ordered to sign the police bail book every day.

Inspector Clive Abela prosecuted.

Lawyers Amadeus Cachia and Ishmael Psaila appeared for Vella, while lawyer Michele Cardinali represented the victim.

Judge Neville Camilleri presided over the Criminal Court.
news.summary: Court hears how accused ran a red light and struck a pedestrian before returning to the scene and speeding past police
news.author: Julia Dowling

news.title: Man remanded in custody after allegedly harassing ex-partner, spitting in her face
news.text:
A man has been remanded in custody after pleading not guilty to a string of 15 charges involving the alleged harassment and threatening of his former partner, as well as breaches of a protection order and bail conditions.

The Albanian national, who resides in Marsaskala and works in construction, pleaded not guilty to the charges brought against him.

The court heard that the police Domestic Violence Unit had received three reports from the accused’s former partner, with whom he has an 11-month-old child. A danger assessment carried out in connection with the reports classified the situation as high risk.

The accused had previously been arraigned on 5 April and granted bail, with a protection order also issued in favour of his former partner. Under the conditions imposed by the court, communication with the woman was restricted to matters concerning their child.

However, the prosecution told the court that three further reports were subsequently filed against him in less than five weeks.

The reports allegedly involved repeated insults and threats, with the prosecution maintaining that communication between the former couple had gone beyond simply discussing their child.

In one alleged incident, the accused asked to see his son in a threatening manner. He is also accused of spitting in his former partner’s face and kicking the passenger door of a vehicle.

The charges also concern repeated calls and electronic communications allegedly made to the woman.

The man is accused of harassing his former partner and causing her to fear that violence would be used against her or her property. He is also charged with breaching the protection order issued in April, threatening or insulting her and making improper use of electronic communications.

Separate charges relate to incidents allegedly occurring in Marsaskala on 27 August and 28 September.

In relation to the August incident, the accused is charged with disturbing the public peace and threatening his former partner with stones or other hard objects, which he allegedly threw towards her vehicle.

He is also accused of disturbing the public peace during the September incident and of throwing filth at the woman.

The prosecution further alleged that the accused had failed to sign his bail book for around four months.

The court was told that police had instructed him on several occasions to attend the police station or Domestic Violence Hub, but that he allegedly failed to comply.

Police eventually located and arrested him on 5 October. The court heard that he allegedly resisted officers, refused to wear handcuffs and shouted during his arrest.

The accused also refused legal assistance when questioned by police and allegedly threw a declaration relating to legal representation onto the floor rather than signing it.

His sister had also suggested a lawyer who could represent him, but he refused.

The man maintained this position during Wednesday’s arraignment, initially telling the court that he did not want to be legally represented because he did not trust anyone to represent him and wanted additional time to find a lawyer.

The court explained that the arraignment had to proceed in accordance with procedure. Legal aid lawyer Martina Herrera represented him during the sitting.

The prosecution also charged the man with breaching the bail conditions imposed in April by allegedly committing further voluntary offences while on bail.

It requested that, in the event of a conviction, his bail be revoked and the €4,000 personal guarantee imposed by the court be forfeited in favour of the government.

Bail denied

A request for bail was made during the sitting.

The prosecution objected, arguing that important witnesses had yet to testify and expressing concern that the accused could not be trusted to observe further bail conditions.

It pointed in particular to his alleged failure to sign the bail book for four months and argued that an existing protection order had allegedly been breached three times in less than five weeks.

The defence stressed the accused remained presumed innocent and had his own version of events.

It argued that he lived separately from the alleged victim, had a stable job and could be subjected to stringent bail conditions and a protection order.

The accused also addressed the court himself, claiming that his former partner spoke to him in the same manner that he spoke to her and arguing that it was unfair that only he was facing prosecution.

After considering the nature of the accusations and the submissions made by the parties, the court denied bail and remanded the accused in custody.

The prosecution was led by Inspector Audrey Micallef. The accused was represented by legal aid lawyer Martina Herrera.

Magistrate Ingrid Bianco presided over the sitting.
news.summary: Prosecution tells court three reports were filed by man’s former partner in less than five weeks, despite an existing protection order
news.author: Julia Dowling

news.title: Ukraine hit by deadly Russian strikes as Putin marks 74th birthday
news.text:
Russia destroyed an apartment block in northern Ukraine as a birthday “gift” to Vladimir Putin, Volodymyr Zelensky said on Wednesday, after overnight missile and drone strikes killed at least 12 people across the country, according to Ukrainian officials.

“Today, as a birthday ‘gift’ to Putin, the Russian army destroyed a residential building in Pryluky, in the Chernihiv region,” the Ukrainian president wrote on social media. Putin turned 74 on Wednesday.

Nine people, including three children, were killed and 34 wounded when a missile hit the five-storey building, Interior Minister Ihor Vyhivskyi said.

“There may still be people under the rubble,” Zelensky said. “First responders are working nonstop at the site – doing everything possible to find every person.”

He said strikes also killed people in Kremenchuk and Oleksandriya and damaged apartment buildings in Dnipro.

Russia’s Defence Ministry confirmed it had carried out a massive overnight strike on industrial facilities involved in producing and storing missiles and drones, as well as port and ship repair facilities in the Odesa region. It made no mention of civilian casualties.

In Kyiv, two people died in a fire caused by the attack in the city’s densely populated Darnytskyi neighbourhood, according to mayor Vitaly Klitschko.

Zelensky described the assault as “one of the most vile strikes” of the nearly five-year conflict. “The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively,” he said.

‘State of fear’

Ukraine’s air force said Russia launched at least 50 missiles and 130 drones overnight at regions including Dnipropetrovsk, Kyiv, Kharkiv and Poltava. It said it intercepted five ballistic missiles, 39 cruise missiles and more than 100 drones.

Zelensky said ballistic missiles were “the greatest challenge” and that new air defences were “a vital necessity”.

He had warned the public on Tuesday night that Russia was preparing a “massive” strike, particularly on energy infrastructure. Kyiv residents spent the night in subway stations with sleeping mats and blankets.

“The whole of Kyiv is in a state of fear,” Iryna Rybalchenko, a bank worker sheltering on a platform, told AFP.

Attacks on the capital have intensified in recent weeks as winter approaches. Scheduled power cuts were introduced on Tuesday to ease pressure on the battered grid, and Klitschko warned last week that the enemy was “tearing Kyiv apart” with strikes on bridges and energy infrastructure.

news.title: Suspect remanded in custody after plane arrest over St Julian’s knife attack
news.text:
Updated at 2:30pm with court developments 

Florent Germain, a 25-year-old car salesman holding dual British and French citizenship, was arraigned in court on Wednesday afternoon over an attempted stabbing in St Julian’s.

The charges include attempted grievous bodily harm but causing slight bodily harm, being in the possession of a bladed weapon without having a license or permit from the Commissioner of Police, as well as breach of public peace.

The case dates back to 1 October at around 3pm, when police received an emergency report of a stabbing in Wilġa Street, St Julian’s. Emergency medical assistance was immediately dispatched to the scene, where the victim was found suffering from stab wounds to his lower back in the kidney area.

Investigators immediately secured and analysed extensive CCTV footage from surrounding properties. Due to the high density of security cameras in the area and clear daylight conditions, police were able to view full, clear footage of the entire incident.

Footage revealed that the accused was operating a rental vehicle, which police traced directly to the suspect.

A magisterial inquiry was launched and an arrest warrant was issued. The court heard that when police followed up on the address provided to the car rental company, they discovered that while the address existed, the suspect did not actually reside there.

To prevent the suspect from fleeing the island, police issued alerts. An alert was triggered on Tuesday morning at 8:30am when the suspect boarded a flight bound for London. Officers moved in immediately, arresting the man on board the aircraft.

The court was informed that the alleged victim has since been arrested for drug possession and is currently remanded in custody.

Germain pleaded not guilty to the charges.

No request for bail was made as the accused lacks a fixed address. Nonetheless, the prosecution requested a protection order for the victim and recommended that the two men be kept in separate prison divisions.

Duty Magistrate Ingrid Bianco accepted both requests.

AG lawyer Joseph Camilleri Azarov prosecuted, together with Inspectors Wayne Camilleri, Pierguido Saliba and Christian Xuereb.

Lawyers Franco Debono, Marion Camilleri and Eman Scicluna represented Germain.
news.summary: Man holding dual British-French citizenship arrested while on plane at Malta International Airport after investigations lead to him as prime suspect in St Julian’s knife attack
news.author: Karl Azzopardi

news.title: Man arrested at airport after St Julian’s stabbing
news.text:
A 25-year-old French man has been arrested at Malta International Airport following several days of investigations into the alleged stabbing of another man in Triq il-Wilġa, St Julian’s.

The incident happened on Thursday 1 October, at about 3 pm, when police were informed an ambulance had been called after a 22-year-old Englishman suffered minor injuries, allegedly caused by a sharp and pointed weapon.

Police investigations and an analysis of CCTV footage showed that, while the victim was walking, another person got out of a vehicle, approached him and then fled the scene.

Investigations continued and, early Tuesday morning, police arrested the alleged attacker as he was about to board a flight to England.

During a search of his luggage, police seized clothing which matched that seen in CCTV footage of the alleged assault.

The man remains in police custody and is expected to appear in court later today at noon.
news.summary: 25-year-old man arrested at Malta International Airport following several days of investigations into the alleged stabbing of another man in Triq il-Wilġa, St Julian’s

news.title: MEPs Want Employers Held Responsible for Workers’ Mental, Physical Health
news.text:
The European Parliament voted Tuesday to urge the European Commission to propose new EU rules aimed at preventing, eliminating or reducing workplace risks that can cause stress, burnout, and mental and physical disorders.

Lawmakers adopted the non-binding legislative initiative report by a vote of 413-210, with 29 abstentions. They said any proposal should be preceded by an impact assessment that includes a review of existing legislation.

Members want employers to be obligated to protect workers’ mental and physical health and ensure safe, dignified working conditions. They also want the Commission and EU countries to explicitly recognize that work-related psychosocial risks can cause occupational diseases.

Violence and harassment

Employers should adopt and carry out policies that define and prohibit violence, harassment, bullying and discriminatory behavior that undermines workers’ dignity or health, lawmakers said. They also called for early detection mechanisms and risk-based prevention protocols for violence by third parties, along with timely support for affected workers.

Risk assessments

Lawmakers recommended that employers regularly assess psychosocial risks, such as excessive workload and high work intensity, and adopt action plans with concrete measures.

They said major restructuring should be subject to a prior risk assessment conducted with workers and their representatives. Examples include teleworking arrangements and the introduction of automated decision-making and monitoring systems.

Employers should ensure that algorithmic management systems do not impose excessive burdens or monitoring on workers, and human oversight must always be maintained, lawmakers said. They also reiterated that workers have a right to disconnect from work.

Returning to work

Workers who have been absent because of psychosocial risks should have a right to a supported and sustainable return, according to the report. Lawmakers recommended that employers create individual return-to-work plans that could include adjustments to working time or work organization and changes to a worker’s tasks or workload.

“Europe must move away from a ‘burnout society’ and help create healthy workplaces where everyone can thrive, especially as the use of digital technologies and AI in the workplace continues to grow,” said Estelle Ceulemans, a Belgian lawmaker with the S&D group who wrote the report. She said the issue also affects public finances “as the cost to society is skyrocketing.”

The Commission has three months to respond. It must either tell Parliament what steps it plans to take or explain why it is refusing to propose legislation along the lines Parliament requested.
