news.title: Man jailed 26 months after stealing mothers car
news.text:
A 23-year-old man has been jailed for 26 months after stealing his mother’s car and leaving her on the ground outside a police station in Birżebbuġa.

Luke Cremona was sentenced after being found guilty of a number of charges arising from a series of incidents in June 2024.

The court heard how, on 19 June 2024, Cremona was travelling with his mother and his girlfriend when an argument broke out between him and the latter.

His mother told the court that Cremona had been under the influence of drugs and alcohol at the time.

After driving to Birżebbuġa, she headed towards the police station as the argument continued. Cremona got out of the vehicle and approached his girlfriend, prompting his mother to also leave the car and attempt to make her way towards the police station while carrying her handbag and car keys.

She testified that her son pushed her from behind, causing her to fall face-first onto the ground.

Cremona then took the keys to her Peugeot 107, which also included keys to her home and apartment block, and drove away.

Members of the public alerted police after seeing the woman on the ground. Officers arrived at the scene, but Cremona had already driven away.

The vehicle was discovered abandoned later that evening in Triq il-Biċċerija, Marsa.

CCTV footage showed two people inside the car arguing shortly after it was parked, with the driver later seen damaging a side mirror. A woman was then seen leaving the vehicle.

The car was subsequently examined by forensic officers, who documented damage to the driver’s side mirror and reddish stains on the vehicle.

Cremona’s mother later told the court that the damage to the car was so extensive that a mechanic advised her it was not worth repairing. She estimated the repairs at around €3,000.

Incident at mother’s home a day earlier

The court also heard that the incident came just one day after Cremona had caused extensive damage inside his mother’s Żurrieq home.

Police had been called to the residence on 18 June following reports of a disturbance.

When Cremona’s mother arrived and allowed officers inside, they found several damaged items, including a television, vacuum cleaner, furniture, a cat scratching pole, rug and other household objects. The damage amounted to €2,485.

Cremona was arrested but was granted police bail the following morning so that he could attend a scheduled meeting with his probation officer.

During a subsequent home visit, probation officer Maryrose Farrugia testified that Cremona was highly agitated and took out a pipe used to consume cocaine, prompting her to immediately terminate the meeting.

Cremona later suggested to his mother that he would pay for the television he had damaged and the two left the house together, eventually leading to the incident in Birżebbuġa.

Cremona admitted to drug problems

During his police statement, Cremona admitted having a drug problem but repeatedly denied assaulting his mother or taking her keys.

“I never touched my mother, and I will never touch my mother,” he told investigators.

However, when he later chose to testify during the proceedings, his version of events changed several times.

He admitted taking and driving the car but initially claimed he had taken the keys from his mother’s handbag at home.

Later, after being confronted with evidence about the Birżebbuġa incident, he said the keys had been left in the ignition and that he drove off after his mother got out of the car.

The court highlighted several inconsistencies in his testimony, with the magistrate at one stage telling him: “Everyone is reminding you, except you.”

Cremona eventually admitted that he had been under the influence of both drugs and alcohol on the day and that he had damaged the car’s side mirror.

He also admitted, after being pressed by the prosecution and the court, that he had driven to Marsa to purchase drugs.

The court described Cremona as an unreliable witness, pointing to the numerous contradictions between his police statement, his testimony and the other evidence before it.

Court rejects argument that taking car was not theft

The defence argued that Cremona’s actions should not amount to theft, but rather the arbitrary exercise of a pretended right.

The court rejected this argument, finding no evidence that Cremona believed he had any right over his mother’s vehicle.

It noted that it was actually Cremona who owed his mother money for the damage he had caused, rather than the other way around.

Although there was no evidence that Cremona intended to sell the vehicle or obtain a financial profit from it, the court explained that the gain required for theft does not necessarily have to be monetary. The benefit he obtained from taking and using the vehicle was sufficient to establish the necessary intention for theft, the court said.

It also rejected the possibility that the case amounted merely to temporary unauthorised use of the car, noting that Cremona did not return it but instead abandoned it in Marsa after damaging it.

The court therefore found the theft charge proven, although it ruled that one of the alleged aggravating factors, theft by means, had not been established because the keys used were not false keys.

Mother asked court to drop case

During proceedings in March 2026, Cremona’s mother told the court that she had forgiven her son and wanted the criminal proceedings against him to stop.

She said they had resolved their differences and that Cremona had reimbursed her for the damage, including €3,000 for the car.

She also told the court that she believed her son regretted what he had done and would not have behaved in that way had he not been under the influence of drugs.

The court, however, explained that her decision could only affect offences which depended on a complaint from the injured party.

Several of the charges, including theft, causing fear of violence and criminal damage, could continue regardless of whether Cremona’s mother wished to pursue the case.

The court consequently acquitted Cremona of the charges of slightly injuring, insulting and assaulting his mother.

Court orders investigation after courtroom admission

The judgment also recounts an unusual exchange which took place while Cremona’s mother was giving evidence.

She told the court that while her son was in prison, he had offered to allow her to withdraw money from his bank account.

Cremona then interrupted her testimony from the dock, saying: “If you don’t testify, I’ll give you the money.”

When the magistrate questioned what he had just said, Cremona confirmed: “That’s what I told her.”

The magistrate immediately ordered the matter to be investigated.

Rehabilitation efforts considered

In determining punishment, the court took into account Cremona’s efforts to address his drug addiction.

His probation officer testified that he had shown a willingness to undergo rehabilitation, while a psychologist who had been following him in prison said he had cooperated and attended sessions aimed at helping him deal with difficult situations without resorting to drugs or gambling.

Caritas representatives also told the court that Cremona had expressed an interest in entering a residential rehabilitation programme.

However, the court also heard that Cremona had received 10 disciplinary reports while in prison since July 2025, including for disobeying officers, fighting and possessing prohibited items.

The court also considered his criminal record, noting that he had previously been convicted of similar offences and had failed to learn from opportunities previously given to him to avoid imprisonment.

26 months in prison

The court ultimately acquitted Cremona of six of the 12 charges against him. He was also cleared of two charges relating to breaching bail conditions after the prosecution failed to exhibit the relevant bail decree, as well as a charge of breaching a protection order after the court found that the evidence did not establish the offence beyond reasonable doubt.

Cremona was nevertheless found guilty of the remaining charges, including aggravated theft of his mother’s vehicle, causing her to fear violence, criminal damage to the vehicle and her home, driving without insurance and failing to comply with police bail.

He was sentenced to 26 months in prison, from which any time already spent in preventive custody in connection with the case is to be deducted.

The court also disqualified Cremona from holding or obtaining a driving licence for 12 months.

Magistrate Donatella Frendo Dimech presided over the court.
news.summary: A 23-year-old man is found guilty of stealing his mother’s car, causing her to fear violence, damaging her property and driving without insurance, despite mother asking court to drop proceedings after forgiving him
news.author: Julia Dowling

news.title: October 7: tensions remain high as conflict rages on
news.text:
Today, 7 October, marks three years since Hamas-led militants launched a surprise attack on Israel shortly after sunrise, firing thousands of rockets from the Gaza Strip and breaching the border fence at dozens of points.

An estimated 6,000 militants crossed into Israel by car, motorbike and paraglider, attacking Israeli communities and military positions in the south.

The assault killed around 1,200 people and saw approximately 250 others taken hostage, triggering Israel’s war in Gaza and a conflict that has since had repercussions across the Middle East.

The attack has been widely recognised as the deadliest single day for Jewish people since the Holocaust.

On the third anniversary, Israelis gathered at memorials in Kfar Aza, Re’im and across the country. Moments of silence were held at 6:29 am, corresponding with the time the attacks began three years earlier.

At the same time, anti-government protesters in Tel Aviv dyed the Dizengoff Square fountain blood-red and displayed hundreds of photographs, flowers and messages.

Demonstrators also blocked major highways, displaying signs and banners describing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as “guilty” and the government’s leadership as a “complete failure”. Protesters also called for a public inquiry into the events surrounding the attack.

Hamas has said the October 7 attack was carried out in response to what it described as the ongoing Israeli occupation of Palestinian territories, the blockade of the Gaza Strip and the detention of Palestinian prisoners in Israeli prisons, among other factors.

The impact on Palestinians has also been severe. According to Gaza’s Health Ministry, at least 74,200 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces over the past three years. Israel has rejected allegations that it is committing genocide, maintaining that its military operations constitute legitimate self-defence, according to NBC.

An estimated 1.9 million people, representing more than 90% of Gaza’s population, have been displaced. Of those, around 1.2 million are reportedly living in tents and shelters, amid increased risks of starvation and disease.

A formal ceasefire was reached around a year ago after both sides accepted US President Donald Trump's 20-point peace plan, raising hopes of an end to the fighting in Gaza. At the time, Malta welcomed Trump’s peace proposal, with the government backing a just peace based on a two-state solution and international law.

Although, Palestinians living in Malta welcomed the prospect of an end to the war, they criticised the plan, arguing that it favoured Israel, excluded Palestinian leadership from negotiations, and did not guarantee Palestinian statehood or equal benefits.

Despite this, hostilities have continued, with more than 1,460 Palestinians reportedly killed in Israeli military strikes since the ceasefire was announced.

Three years later, Gaza bears little resemblance to the territory that existed before the war. Concerns have grown that large-scale and potentially permanent displacement could become entrenched, amid questions over the absence of sufficient political and military mechanisms to prevent it.
news.summary: From protests to memorials, Isreal is forced to remember the attacks that left over 1,200 civilians dead three years ago on October 7 by Hamas, also resulting in over 74,200 Palestinian deaths since
news.author: Jade Bezzina

news.title: A five-decade journey from design to painting
news.text:
A career spanning graphic design, teaching and painting will come together in From Design to Light, a solo exhibition opening at the St John Ambulance & Rescue HQ in Valletta on Friday 16 October 2026.

The exhibition brings together work from across five decades, tracing Doranne Alden’s journey from her early training in art and professional career in graphic design to a life devoted to painting. Around 25 to 30 framed works will be on display, combining a retrospective selection with more recent paintings.

Michael Frendo will officially open the exhibition at 7.30pm on Friday 16 October. The exhibition will run from 17 to 31 October and is the first exhibition to be held at the St John Ambulance & Rescue HQ.

The title, From Design to Light, reflects two disciplines that have remained closely connected throughout the artist’s life. Although graphic design became her profession from an early age, painting was never abandoned. “I have always been a watercolourist,” Alden says. She describes painting not as something she returned to later in life, but as a constant thread running through her career.

Alden began learning art at around the age of 14 at Msida Polytechnic. At 18, she entered the world of graphic design, where she initially worked with Promotion Services and Rowland Phototypesetting before joining JPA Advertising at 21.

During her years at JPA, she worked on the original design and paste-up of Circle Magazine. She overaw its design during its first five years. She became head designer at approximately 24, before co-founding Details Design Ltd in 1990.

In 1995, Alden moved to Germany, where she taught painting and held exhibitions. Following her return to Malta in 2003, she continued teaching and exhibiting, while also developing a programme of painting activities. Since 2012, she has organised painting weekends and painting holidays in Gozo, as well as painting trips abroad, including group trips to Tuscany.

The exhibition brings together these different strands of her career, looking at the development of her work over five decades while also reflecting the places, experiences and memories that have informed her painting.

Among the works on display is the title painting, Catching Fishing Bait, Golden Bay (2026). The selection also includes paintings inspired by Malta and Gozo, alongside works drawn from places and memories accumulated over the years, including Comino Channel, Red Vespa, Mum’s Heavenly Terrace, The Orange Orchard in Buskett and Prickly Pear Delight.

The retrospective section opens with Freesia in Orange Vase, offering an entry point into a body of work that spans decades and demonstrates the continuing relationship between observation, design and the possibilities of watercolour.
news.summary: ​A career spanning graphic design, teaching and painting will come together in From Design to Light, a solo exhibition opening at the St John Ambulance & Rescue HQ in Valletta on Friday 16 October 2026
news.author: Laura Calleja

news.title: Diplomats: Deaths from Russian-linked hybrid attacks are a matter of when, not if
news.text:
Diplomats from the 27 European Union countries are privately working out how the bloc would respond to a hybrid attack that kills several people, a scenario five EU diplomats and officials told POLITICO is looking more likely.

The planning has also exposed disagreement over how big a security role the EU should play and whether its work overlaps with NATO’s, according to the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss confidential talks.

EU ambassadors have taken up the issue in recent weeks in a “restricted format” that bars phones and assistants. The talks intensified after an explosives-laden drone was found at Leipzig airport in August. Two diplomats said ambassadors met last Wednesday to focus on mass-casualty examples.

The EU has long discussed hybrid threats, which it and NATO define as subversive activity short of an act of war. It has a “hybrid toolbox” for responding to cyberattacks, election interference and sabotage. The EU says Russia has stepped up cyberattacks, sabotage and covert operations across the bloc since invading Ukraine.

The latest discussions have centered on sending emergency response teams, freeing up EU funds to help an affected country and deciding how EU leaders should communicate, one official said.

“We have to be prepared for something serious,” a senior EU diplomat said. A second official said casualties are “bound” to occur and that none so far was “sheer luck.”

Recent incidents include the Leipzig drone, a suspicious fire at a Polish ground station that handles Starlink communications and a plot to plant incendiary devices at transport hubs in the EU and U.K. Bulgarian officials said Tuesday that several sailors were missing after drones sank their ship in the Black Sea.

Teija Tiilikainen, director of the European Centre of Excellence for Countering Hybrid Threats, said Russia is using increasingly lethal tools and that deaths will eventually follow. A NATO diplomat said the death of an allied citizen would put heavy pressure on both organizations to act.

Some capitals say the EU is overstepping and duplicating NATO. Oana Lungescu, a former NATO spokesperson now at the Royal United Services Institute, warned that overlap could slow decisions. Several diplomats also cited the EU’s lack of secure communications and fears of leaks, including reports that Hungary’s former foreign minister relayed leader-level talks to his Russian counterpart. A diplomat from an eastern flank country said sensitive intelligence is kept out of EU settings for that reason.

The debate coincides with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s push for an “emergency security protocol” and a “European Security Council.” Two diplomats said both are expected in a European Security Strategy due in early November. Several diplomats said the measures would take months to set up and duplicate existing tools, such as the Integrated Political Response mechanism.

Under that mechanism, the rotating EU presidency can call emergency meetings at an affected country’s request. France invoked the EU’s mutual assistance clause, Article 42.7, after the 2015 Bataclan attacks, the only time it has been used. Lungescu called that a political decision that produced little beyond coordinated investigations.

She said NATO should handle intelligence-sharing and military deterrence while the EU focuses on civilian response. She added that Russian President Vladimir Putin does not distinguish between the two organizations.

news.title: Israelis mark three years since Hamas attack that set off Gaza assault
news.text:
Israelis will on Wednesday mark three years since Hamas attacked Israel on ​October 7, 2023, triggering a military assault that destroyed much of Gaza, where conditions remain dire despite a year-old ceasefire that is ‌meant to halt the war for good.

The attacks, during which militants killed 1,200 people and took 251 hostages to Gaza, marked the deadliest day in Israel’s history. Israel’s subsequent bombardment and ground operations have killed more than 74,000 people in Gaza, health authorities there say.

On Wednesday, Israelis will hold a vigil at the site of the Nova music ​festival near the Gaza border, where 348 young people were killed by militants during the attack.

They will also hold an event commemorating ​the anniversary at Hostage Square in Tel Aviv.

ISRAELI ELECTION 20 DAYS AWAY

The anniversary is the first for Israelis without ⁠any hostages still held in Gaza, with those dead and alive exchanged in swaps with Hamas for Palestinians held in Israeli jails. The remains ​of the last Israeli hostage were recovered in January.

It also comes just 20 days ahead of Israel’s first election since the attack, a vote ​that is viewed as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s long tenure in power.

Netanyahu has rejected blame for the security breach and resisted calls for an independent investigation. That has frustrated many in Israel, including families of those killed in the attacks, some of whom have joined the election race.

Item 1 of 5 A woman visits the site of the Nova music festival, where partygoers were killed and kidnapped during the deadly Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack, on the third anniversary of the attack, near Reim, southern Israel, October 7, 2026. REUTERS/Ronen Zvulun

[1/5]A woman visits the site of the Nova music festival, where partygoers were killed and kidnapped during the deadly Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack, on the third anniversary of the attack, near Reim, southern Israel, October 7, 2026. REUTERS/Ronen Zvulun Purchase Licensing Rights, opens new tab

A poll by the Israel Democracy Institute showed ​that 68% of Jewish Israelis said that the events of October 7 were a very central or fairly central element in their decision of ​which party to vote for.

Election polls show neither Netanyahu nor his main competitors would muster enough seats in parliament to form a coalition if a vote were ‌held today.

US-BACKED ⁠CEASEFIRE FAILS TO HALT ISRAELI ATTACKS, DISARM HAMAS

The anniversary is also the first since an October 10, 2025, US-brokered ceasefire deal that halted major fighting but has failed to stop Israeli attacks in Gaza or secure the disarmament of Hamas and other militant groups.

The deal left Israel in control of some 53% of Gaza, since expanded by Israeli forces to nearly two-thirds. Hamas controls the remaining third, where the 2 million population mostly live in makeshift tents ​and bombed out buildings.

US President Donald ​Trump’s so-called “Board of Peace” has proposed ⁠several plans that would see Gaza rebuilt. But those plans, which fail to account for the property rights of Palestinians whose homes were destroyed, have failed to gain the buy-in of Israel or Hamas, which are ​still deadlocked in ceasefire talks.

The two have yet to agree on the terms of a deal that would ​see Hamas lay down ⁠its weapons in exchange for Israeli troop withdrawals. Israel says it will not pull back until Hamas fully disarms; Hamas says it has agreed to a phased process but will not disarm so long as Israeli attacks continue.

Israel has kept up a bombing campaign in Gaza that has killed a number of ⁠Hamas militants ​in recent months but has also killed many civilians, say Gaza health authorities, whose ​death figures do not distinguish between civilians and combatants.

More than 1,400 Palestinians in Gaza have been killed since the October 2025 ceasefire, the health authorities say. During the same time, five ​Israeli soldiers have been killed by militants or in combat, the military says.

Source: Reuters

news.title: Objecting to the use of the penthouse roof. Check your contract first!
news.text:
In a recent case decided by Judge Aaron Bugeja, the Civil Court had to determine the right of use of a penthouse roof to install a water tank, a water pump, airconditioning compressor and solar panels.

These matters are normally spelled out in the deed of acquisition but notwithstanding the penthouse owner insisted no use could be made of the roof of his penthouse to install a water tank and pump, an AC compressor and photovoltaic panels.

There was no dispute as to ownership of the penthouse roof. It belonged to the owner of the penthouse. What was at issue was whether the plaintiff had exclusive use of the said roof and so absolute control over what takes place on it, or whether the deed of acquisition placed any limitation on the use of the roof by the owner in the form of servitudes in favour of the underlying apartments.

In its judgment the court observed that the plaintiff’s deed of acquisition explained clearly the division of real rights, which the original vendors—the developers of the block—had drawn up. Once such deed outlines the burdens and restrictions of use. By signing such a deed, the plaintiff was expressly consenting to a restriction of use on his roof. Furthermore, the deed of acquisition was supplemented with a plan, which outlined the manner in which the roof was divided for this use. Therefore, when the original vendor sold the remaining units, he was not creating any new rights but rather allocating to the beneficiary the right of use already specified in the deed of acquisition of the plaintiff.

The court pointed out that the plaintiff had given a very partial reading of the deed of acquisition of his penthouse. The deed expressly stated that the deed incorporates the contract as well as all documents annexed to it. On this basis, the court gave weight to the plan of the roof attached to the deed. The plan outlined which apartment had exclusive use of which area on the roof. The court concluded that acceptance of the plan by the penthouse owner signalled his acceptance that he did not have absolute use of the roof.

The judgment states that there is a difference between the right to property and the right of use of the roof of the same property. The latter in legal jargon is known as the jus utendi, and in this case it was not absolute to the owner of the penthouse. The right of use of the penthouse owner in this case was limited to one area while other areas were allocated to other apartments including to the owner of the penthouse.

The fact that the penthouse or apartment was not yet in a complete state does not mean that the parties could not create, reserve or regulate real rights, easements or restrictions on the basis of plans and conditions integrated into the contracts. Contract law does not prohibit a future property, airspace or shell form from being transferred with clear conditions as to its future use. The court referred to the legal principle pacta sunt servanda, found in Article 992 of the Maltese Civil Code. It means that a contract legally entered into shall have the force of law for the contracting parties, and the parties may only depart from the obligations entered into if there is a revocation by mutual consent, or on grounds allowed by law.

The court rejected the claims by the plaintiff that there were no servitudes burdening the use of the penthouse roof and allowed the defendant—the owner of the underlying apartment—to place a water tank, a water pump, an airconditioning compressor and PV panels on the roof.

The judgment was appealed. Lawyers Paul Radmilli and Cedric Mifsud appeared for the defendant.
news.summary: In a recent case decided by Judge Aaron Bugeja, the Civil Court had to determine the right of use of a penthouse roof to install a water tank, a water pump, airconditioning compressor and solar panels

news.title: Second block of flats approved beside medieval Dingli chapel
news.text:
The Planning Commission has approved an eight-apartment development metres away from Dingli’s medieval Santa Duminka Chapel.

This is the second development approved near the Grade 1 scheduled building despite objections over the impact on the chapel’s archaeological setting.

The application (PA/07782/24), submitted by Brian Azzopardi, involves excavation of the site, three basement garages and eight dwellings in Triq il-Kappella Medjevali. The Planning Commission voted 2-0 in favour.

The site lies within the chapel’s archaeological buffer zone. Objectors argued that the project failed to properly assess the chapel’s wider setting. Furthermore, the Dingli Local Council also objected because of the scheduled building.

The development forms part of a broader process that has opened up this previously inaccessible area of Dingli to residential construction.

Although the area was already within the development zone, construction had been hampered by the lack of road access. Infrastructure Malta constructed Triq il-Kappella Medjevali in 2021, along a road that had been schemed in local plans since the 1960s.

The road was constructed without a planning permit because it was already included in the local plans and a 2008 legal notice exempts state bodies from seeking permits for schemed roads.

Infrastructure Malta said the road was needed to provide access for fire engines and emergency services, while Moviment Graffitti, which organised protests against the road’s construction, warned it would facilitate further development around the historic chapel.

In fact, six years later the site of the new development is now separated from the chapel by the new road.

The first residential application was filed in October 2023 for a block of nine flats on an adjacent site. The Superintendent of Cultural Heritage (SCH) initially objected because of its impact on the chapel. The proposal was subsequently scaled down by removing one full floor and was eventually approved.

Azzopardi’s application was the second residential project to be proposed along the new road. When presented in November 2024, it envisaged nine flats in a five-storey block with a rooftop pool. The plans were subsequently revised to eight dwellings.

The approved project consists of three full floors and a further receded penthouse level.

The PA said the stepped design would minimise the volumes visually affecting the chapel. The SCH raised no objection to the latest plans, subject to archaeological monitoring.

The basement will contain three garages, despite the eight apartments requiring eight parking spaces. The developer will therefore pay €23,000 into the Urban Improvements Fund for the five-space shortfall.
news.summary: The Planning Commission has approved an eight-apartment development metres away from Dingli’s medieval Santa Duminka Chapel
news.author: James Debono

news.title: Only 16% expected Yorgen Fenech acquittal, MaltaToday survey finds
news.text:
Only 16.1% of people said they expected Yorgen Fenech to be acquitted, while 40.8% said they did not expect the verdict, a MaltaToday survey shows. 

Respondents were asked whether they expected Yorgen Fenech’s not-guilty verdict. They were also given the option of stating that they had not followed the case, did not know, or did not want to answer. 

Fenech was acquitted of complicity in the wilful homicide of Daphne Caruana Galizia and of associating with a person or persons for the purpose of committing a crime. A nine-member jury returned an 8-1 not-guilty verdict on both counts. 

The verdict, delivered on 2 September after a 55-day trial, came as a surprise to many and triggered public protests and expressions of disbelief and anger, including from Caruana Galizia’s family. The Attorney General has since filed an appeal against the acquittal. 

The MaltaToday survey, which included other questions that will be published on Sunday, was carried out between Tuesday 22 September and Friday 2 October 2026. The survey has a margin of error of ±3.4 percentage points. 

The findings point to a substantial level of disengagement, with 24.9% saying they had not followed the case, while a further 7.8% said they did not know what to make of the verdict and 10.5% declined to answer. 

The refusal rate is notable, suggesting that a tenth of respondents may have been reluctant to express a view on a case that remains highly sensitive and polarising, although the survey does not establish the reasons for this reluctance. 

72% of those who answered did not expect Fenech acquittal 

Among respondents, who gave one of the two substantive answers to the question (56.9%), 71.7% said they had not expected Fenech to be acquitted, while 28.3% said they had expected the verdict. 

In other words, among those who expressed a definite view, more than seven in 10 did not see the acquittal coming, compared with fewer than three in 10 who said they had expected it. These figures provide a clearer picture of expectations among respondents who were willing to express a view on the verdict. 

Majority of PL voters do not express an opinion 

A majority of PL voters did not give a definite opinion on whether they expected the not-guilty verdict. Of those who voted for the PL in the last general election, 31% said they had not followed the case, 9.7% did not know and 10.9% refused to answer. Only 13.7% said they had expected the verdict, while 34.7% said they had not. 

Among PN voters, 19.5% said they had expected the not-guilty verdict, compared with 50.9% who said they had not expected it. Only 5.3% said they did not know, while 9% refused to answer. A further 15.4% said they had not followed the case. 

Once those who had not followed the case, did not know or refused to answer are excluded, the difference between the two main parties largely disappears. Among PL voters who gave one of the two definitive answers, 71.7% said they had not expected the acquittal, compared with 28.3% who had expected it. Among PN voters who gave a definite answer, 72.2% said they had not expected the verdict, compared with 27.8% who had expected it. 

Among those who did not vote in the last election, 13.2% expected the acquittal, while 28.7% did not. The largest group in this category, 34.3%, said they had not followed the case. Another 9.8% did not know and 13.9% declined to answer. 

Small-party voters recorded a similar pattern to PN voters, with 19.6% saying they had expected the verdict and 59.2% saying they had not. Only 12.2% said they had not followed the case, while 2.6% did not know and 6.3% refused to answer. 

The figures also show a marked difference in engagement with the trial. PN voters were more likely to have followed the case and to give a definite response than PL voters or those who did not vote. 

Among PN voters, 29.6% either had not followed the case, did not know or refused to answer. The corresponding figure among PL voters was 51.7%, meaning that more than half of those who had voted Labour in the last election did not provide a definite answer. Among those who did not vote, the figure was even higher, at 58%. 

This difference in engagement helps explain why the raw figures show a wider gap between PN and PL voters. PN voters were considerably more likely to have followed the case and provide a definite response. 

Women less keen on trial 

There was little difference between men and women in expectations of the verdict. 

16.7% of men said they had expected the acquittal, compared with 15.4% of women. 

However, women were substantially more likely to say they had not followed the case—28.9% compared with 20.9% of men. 

The proportion saying, they had not expected the verdict was also higher among men, at 44.6%, than among women, at 37%. 

There was virtually no difference in refusal rates, with 10.5% of women and 10.4% of men declining to answer. 

29% of younger respondents did not follow the case 

The 36–50 age group was the most likely to say it had expected the acquittal, at 21.4%. 

This was followed by those aged 51–65 at 16.3%, while 14.9% of those aged 16–35 and 12% of those over 65 said they had expected the verdict. 

The youngest group had the highest proportion saying they had not followed the case, at 29%, while the figure among those aged 36–50 was 19.9%. 

Respondents over 65 were the least likely to say they had expected the verdict and the most likely age group to answer “don't know”, at 9.6%. 

Regional differences 

There were also differences between regions. The Southern Harbour, traditionally a strong Labour region, recorded the highest proportion expecting the acquittal of the business tycoon, at 18.6%, followed by the Western region at 18%, Northern Harbour at 17.2%, Gozo at 16.5%, Northern at 14.2% and the South Eastern region at 11.3%, the lowest figure among all regions. 

In contrast, the Northern region stood out for the proportion saying they had not expected the verdict, at 50.1%, followed by Northern Harbour at 47.4%, South Eastern at 40.2%, Gozo at 36.8%, Western at 34.3% and Southern Harbour at 30.8%. 

But the survey suggests a divergence in reactions to the verdict between the two Labour-leaning southern regions. 

In the South Eastern region, only 11.3% said they had expected the acquittal, while 40.2% said they had not expected it, almost four times as many. By contrast, in the Southern Harbour, 18.6% expected the verdict and 30.8% did not. The difference suggests that respondents in the South Eastern region were considerably more likely to say the verdict had surprised them. 

The South Eastern region also had a relatively high proportion who said they had not followed the case, at 29.2%, second only to the Southern Harbour at 30.1%. A further 8.1% said they did not know and 11.2% declined to answer. 

In all, 48.5% of respondents in the South Eastern region either had not followed the case, did not know or refused to answer. 

Gozo recorded 16.5% who expected the acquittal, while 36.8% said they had not expected it. However, 21.3% said they had not followed the case, while 9.4% did not know and 16% declined to answer, the highest refusal rate among all regions. 

Verdict surprised more than it didn’t 

Overall, the survey shows that the acquittal was substantially more likely to have been unexpected than expected among those who engaged with the question. 

But the findings also point to a second feature of public reaction—a sizeable proportion either did not follow the case, did not know how to answer or chose not to express a view. 

The 10.5% refusal rate, in particular, suggests that for some reason a significant minority were reluctant to talk about their expectations of the Fenech verdict.
news.summary: MaltaToday survey: 16.1% expected not-guilty verdict, 40.8% did not expect it, 7.8% do not know, 24.9% did not follow case and 10.5% declined to answer

news.title: A law criminalising mafia association does not equate to having a mafia state
news.text:
One of the recommendations made by the Daphne Caruana Galizia Public Inquiry was to introduce a new offence in the Criminal Code dealing with mafia-style association.

The recommendation was modelled on Article 416-bis of the Italian Criminal Code, which makes mere membership of a mafia-style criminal organisation an offence punishable with imprisonment of between 10 and 15 years. Those who promote, direct or organise the association shall be punished, for that alone, with imprisonment of between 12 and 18 years.

The rationale behind such a legal provision is to give law enforcement agencies an additional tool to fight serious organised crime by attacking it at its core—mere membership.

Unfortunately, like the vast majority of the recommendations made by the public inquiry, this proposal was never implemented. But what stands out about this recommendation is Prime Minister Robert Abela’s Talebanesque opposition to it based on reasons that defy logic.

On Tuesday, during a heated exchange in parliament with Opposition leader Alex Borg, the prime minister reiterated his complete disagreement with introducing the mafia association offence because it would convey the message that Malta is a mafia state.

“I totally, disagree because our country is not a mafia state… I have said it before and will say it again that I do not agree with a provision that suggests Malta is a mafia state and as long as I am prime minister it will never be introduced,” Abela told parliament.

But this is where Abela’s logic is warped. Adopting the same reasoning, Malta is a terrorist state because it has anti-terrorism provisions in its Criminal Code. By no stretch of the imagination is Malta a terrorist state and yet, as a country that understands the ugly cross-border and domestic impact of terrorism it felt the need to legislate accordingly.

Introducing a new provision in the Criminal Code that makes membership of a mafia-style association an offence does not, in any way, mean Malta is a mafia state. On the contrary, it is one way of showing willingness to fight organised crime in every way possible. It will give the police more tools to go after these organisations and dismantle them. It creates a deterrent for those toying with the idea of being part of these criminal organisations.

But what is more perplexing with Abela’s stand is that he is concerned about the reputational damage such a law could create but seemingly unperturbed by the reputational damage caused by what emerged from Yorgen Fenech’s trial.

The trial showed how during the Joseph Muscat years, the boundaries between politics, business and criminality got blurred to the point that a climate of impunity resulted in the assassination of Daphne Caruana Galizia. The evidence presented in court raised serious questions about the conduct of people in public office and their proximity with businesspersons and shady characters. The evidence showed how sensitive information about the murder investigation was being leaked to Fenech from inside Castille.

What emerged was a shocking picture, which had all the makings of a mafia-style association.

Abela should take heed of what Labour Party President Alex Sciberras said over the weekend: “We cannot pretend to have heard nothing.”

And while the actions of individuals do not define the Labour Party and its members, the party cannot simply walk away from the proverbial scene of the crime and pretend nothing happened. Implementing the public inquiry recommendations is one way for the PL to atone for the actions of those who, acting in its name, had a finger in Caruana Galizia’s murder.

The introduction of the mafia association offence should be the least of Abela’s worries. He should embrace such a proposal because one of the lessons learnt from the Fenech trial was the need to modernise our legislation and introduce new offences.

The state must not have its hands shackled by outdated or inadequate laws when it is fighting sophisticated organised crime networks that even operate across borders. This does not equate to calling Malta a mafia state but rather represents a modern state where the forces of law and order are given all the necessary tools to carry out their fight against crime without fear or favour.
news.summary: Unfortunately, like the vast majority of the recommendations made by the public inquiry, this proposal was never implemented. But what stands out about this recommendation is Prime Minister Robert Abela’s Talebanesque opposition to it based on reasons that defy logic

news.title: Malta News Briefing – Wednesday 7 October 2026
news.text:
Morning Briefing

Tax officials to contact hundreds over suspected tax evasion

Tax officials are preparing to contact “hundreds” of people suspected of tax evasion over unexplained discrepancies between their declared income and spending, Finance Minister Clyde Caruana has said. Letters are expected to be sent in the coming weeks to people whose reported income appears inconsistent with their financial activity. These include businesses reporting high turnover while declaring incomes close to the minimum wage, as well as low earners who have purchased expensive assets. The Finance Minister added the tax authorities were using artificial intelligence to analyse tax records across the country and identify potential cases for further investigation. Minister Caruana said those contacted would be asked to explain the apparent discrepancies and regularise their position where necessary. The initiative forms part of wider efforts to improve tax compliance and tackle undeclared income and wealth. (Times of Malta)

Malta’s first Building Codes nearing completion

Work on Malta’s first Building Codes is nearing completion, with a public consultation on the new rules expected to begin in the coming months, Infrastructure, Planning and Employment Minister Jonathan Attard has said. Attard said the initial work on the codes was being concluded while the government continued discussions with the Chamber of Architects and other stakeholders. Speaking during a visit to an exhibition organised by SACES, the student organisation representing architecture students within the Faculty for the Built Environment, he described the codes as an important development that would have a significant impact on the construction sector. The minister encouraged professionals and students to participate in upcoming consultations on reforms affecting the industry. He also highlighted measures introduced in recent years to raise construction standards, including new health and safety rules, stronger enforcement and joint inspections by the Occupational Health and Safety Authority and Building and Construction Authority. Other reforms include the licensing of builders and contractors. (The Malta Independent)

Outdoor sports policy follows earlier developer discussions

A proposed planning policy allowing temporary outdoor sports facilities on rural land was discussed with developers as early as 2023, documents show. The Planning Authority is currently consulting on a draft Planning and Design Framework for Temporary Outdoor Sports Events and Facilities, following instructions from then Planning Minister Clint Camilleri in April. The consultation runs until October 10. Such recreational activities are currently not generally permitted in outside development zone areas, where development is largely restricted to agricultural and agritourism uses. The policy follows earlier discussions surrounding a proposed 39,000-square-metre obstacle course at Ta’ Qali. During a Planning Authority hearing in July 2023, the developers’ architect requested that the application be suspended, saying discussions were taking place with government entities on policies and guidance for outdoor sports facilities. At the time, the authority said it had not been formally notified of any policy revision. (Maltatoday)
